name: River Gambia National Park
blurb: Baboon Islands: riverside forest, manatees, hippos and reintroduced chimps.

tip.title: Remove the chimpanzees
tip.text: Chimpanzees hunt red colobus and baboons. Select them and lower their numbers, then watch the monkeys that fed them and the trees those monkeys eat.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Oil palm
nodes.desc: A palm whose fruit feeds many animals. GBIF records show it in the area, and palm-nut vultures, chimpanzees and monkeys are all recorded eating it.

nodes.name: Raphia palm
nodes.desc: A palm of wet ground whose fruit is eaten by chimpanzees and baboons, and is a main food of palm-nut vultures.

nodes.name: Silk cotton tree
nodes.desc: A very tall forest tree. Its flowers and fruit are eaten by fruit bats.

nodes.name: Riverside forest trees
nodes.desc: Trees of the wet riverbank forest whose leaves and overhanging branches feed monkeys and manatees.

nodes.name: Wild rice & riverbank grasses
nodes.desc: Wild rice and other grasses growing on wet, flooded ground. Hippos graze on grasses.

nodes.name: Water lotus
nodes.desc: A floating water plant of slow river channels and backwaters.

nodes.name: Western red colobus
nodes.desc: A leaf-eating monkey of forest treetops. Wikipedia says common chimpanzees frequently hunt it.

nodes.name: Green monkey
nodes.desc: A common, widely recorded monkey of the area that feeds on fruit and other plant foods.

nodes.name: Guinea baboon
nodes.desc: An opportunistic omnivore that eats fruit, roots, seeds, leaves and some small animals. Chimpanzees have been seen preying on it in Senegal.

nodes.name: Gambian epauletted fruit bat
nodes.desc: A fruit bat recorded feeding on silk cotton tree. It likely helps spread seeds and pollen.

nodes.name: West African manatee
nodes.desc: Lives in the Gambia River. River manatees mostly eat vegetation overhanging the banks and have few natural enemies besides crocodiles and people.

nodes.name: Hippopotamus
nodes.desc: Wikipedia says some hippos remain in the park, though they are now rare in the Gambia. They graze on land at night and rest in water by day.

nodes.name: Tilapia & other cichlids
nodes.desc: River fish that feed on plants and algae. They are the main prey for fish-eating birds and reptiles.

nodes.name: African fish eagle
nodes.desc: Hunts fish from a perch over open water, also takes waterbirds, and will eat carrion.

nodes.name: Palm-nut vulture
nodes.desc: An unusual vulture that eats mostly oil palm and raphia fruit, with some fish, crabs, small animals and carrion.

nodes.name: Nile monitor
nodes.desc: A large water-loving lizard that hunts along the river and eats fish and other animals.

nodes.name: Nile crocodile
nodes.desc: Wikipedia lists crocodiles among the reptiles of the park. Crocodiles take fish and are the main natural enemy of manatees in West Africa.

nodes.name: Common chimpanzee
nodes.desc: A reintroduced population lives on the Baboon Islands. Chimpanzees eat fruit and also hunt monkeys such as red colobus and Guinea baboons.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Tropical sun drives plant growth year round.

nodes.name: Rainy season
nodes.desc: Seasonal rain raises the river and floods low ground, and manatees move up rivers in the wet season.

nodes.name: Gambia River
nodes.desc: The slow, wide river that holds the islands of the park and supports water plants, fish and wet forest.

nodes.name: River soil
nodes.desc: Damp, flooded riverbank soil that feeds palms, trees and grasses.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, termites and bacteria that break down leaves, fallen fruit and dead animals.
